subject: mongol horsemen
title: Genghis Khan's Wars Pulled 700 Million Tons of Carbon From the Sky

scenes.text: One man's wars cooled the whole planet.
Genghis Khan and his heirs conquered from China to Eastern Europe. Historians estimate about 40 million people died between 1200 and 1380.
In 2011, scientists at the Carnegie Institution did something strange with that history. They checked what it did to the air.
Across the emptied land, abandoned farms grew back into forest. Those trees pulled about 700 million tons of carbon out of the atmosphere.
That is roughly as much carbon as the whole world's gasoline burning puts out in a year today.
The Black Death killed a bigger share of Europe, but it was too short: the forests never got time to grow back. Only the Mongols lasted long enough to change the sky.

description:
The Mongol conquests cooled the planet: forests regrowing on emptied farmland pulled about 700 million tons of carbon out of the air.
A 2011 study by Julia Pongratz and colleagues at the Carnegie Institution's Department of Global Ecology modelled the carbon effect of history's great die-offs. The Mongol invasion of Asia (1200-1380), with roughly 40 million dead, let enough farmland return to forest to absorb about 700 million tons of carbon, close to the world's annual carbon emissions from gasoline today. The Black Death, the fall of the Ming dynasty and the conquest of the Americas were too short for regrown forests to make a lasting dent.
Which other event in history do you think left a mark on the planet itself?
first_comment: The same study found that human farming had been adding carbon to the air for centuries before the first steam engine. Which event in history do you think changed the planet most?
